titulo: Balance: center of mass and support polygon
lead: A standing humanoid is an inverted pendulum on two small feet. In this lesson you calculate the G1's center of mass, support polygon, and center of pressure from the model itself, push the robot with different forces, and separate three things that usually get mixed up: leaving the support, swaying, and falling.
objetivo: push the G1 and say, from the simulation, when the center of mass leaves the support polygon and whether the robot falls.

aprende.t: Center of mass, support polygon, and center of pressure (ZMP on flat ground)
CoM margin in centimeters, every 0.25 s
Why 25 N leaves the support and comes back, and 35 N knocks it down
Where classical control (ZMP) and RL come in

hero_alt: Standing humanoid robot in a dark lab being pushed by a padded pole, with a safety cable attached to the gantry.

secoes.titulo: Four quantities, one question: does it fall?

nos.detalhe: The average of all body positions, weighted by mass. MuJoCo computes it in d.subtree_com; the pelvis one is the whole robot's. At rest, the G1's sits 0.69 m above the floor (lesson 8).

The smallest convex polygon that contains every point of the feet touching the ground with force. With both feet on the ground, it is the area between them; with one foot on its toes, it shrinks to a line.

itens.t: average of the contacts, weighted by force

nos.detalhe: The center of pressure is the midpoint of the contacts, weighted by the normal force. On flat ground, it coincides with the ZMP of classical controllers. It never leaves the polygon: when it touches the edge, the foot starts to rotate.

CoM outside the support for an instant does not make it fall: the robot rolls over the edge of the foot and can come back. What makes it fall is rotating too fast to come back. The equilibrio.py calls a fall the pelvis below 0.5 m at t = 3 s (the torque_agachado.py from lesson 4 uses 0.4 m, because when squatting the pelvis already drops to 0.59 m).

secoes.legenda: Standing still, it is enough for the CoM to be inside the support. In motion, the CoP and the speed are what matter.

secoes.sub: A 0.2 s forward push on the torso, with the G1 just holding the pose. Click each band.

texto: The CoM never leaves the polygon: the margin never goes negative at any moment.
That is what any rigid pose can handle: the impulse is small (3 N·s).
The robot rises onto its toes, the polygon becomes a line, and the CoM is outside it for a moment. Even so, it comes back and ends up standing.
Leaving the support is not falling: it is starting to rotate.
At 40 N the CoM leaves at t = 0.73 s; the robot sways forward, comes back, overshoots, and falls backward, without moving a foot.
A balance controller would take a step or move the hip and ankle. Here there is no controller: it is the limit of the body alone.
Classical controllers plan the ZMP to stay inside the support (centroidal models, MPC). Humanoid locomotion in research today is trained with RL in thousands of parallel simulations (course 1).
The training's research found, as of 10/2026, no independent comparison saying which one is better: the two coexist.

secoes.sub: The equilibrio.py applies the force on the torso at t = 0.5 s and prints, every 0.25 s, the CoM margin (positive = inside the support), the CoP forward, and the pelvis height.

blocos.conteudo:
F=${FTH:-$HOME/fth}; cd $F/anatomia && . $F/.venv/bin/activate
for n in 10 15 20 25 30 35 40; do
  echo "$n N → $(python3 kit/equilibrio.py --empurrao $n | tail -2 | cut -d'(' -f1 | tr '\n' ' ')"
done

From 20 to 30 N the CoM leaves the support and the robot does not fall. Anyone who measures balance only by the CoM position gets it wrong from 20 to 30 N; you also need to look at the speed and what happens afterward.

secoes.sub: Find the limit of the body without a controller.

exercicios.titulo: E1 · A push that knocks it over
exercicios.texto: Run the 40 N block and describe the motion by reading the CoP and pelvis columns.
exercicios.pronto: python3 kit/equilibrio.py --empurrao 40 ends with CoM dentro do apoio: não · saiu em t = 0.73 s and queda: sim.

exercicios.titulo: E2 · A push it can handle
exercicios.pronto: python3 kit/equilibrio.py --empurrao 15 | tail -2 → CoM dentro do apoio: sim (o tempo todo) and queda: não.

exercicios.texto: Run 40 N for 0.1 s and 80 N for 0.1 s. Compare with 40 N for 0.2 s: what matters, the force or the product of force × time?
exercicios.pronto: --empurrao 40 --duracao 0.1 ends with queda: não and --empurrao 80 --duracao 0.1 with queda: sim; you wrote down the three impulses (4, 8 and 8 N·s).

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after you answer.

perguntas.p: With 25 N the CoM left the support polygon, but the robot ended up standing. How do you explain that?
opcoes: The script got the support polygon calculation wrong in this case.
It rotated over the edge of the foot at low speed and came back.
MuJoCo stops computing the CoM after the first second.
The support polygon grew and reached the CoM again.
perguntas.explica: Outside the support, the body starts to rotate over the edge. If the speed is low, gravity brings it back. Leaving the support is not falling.

perguntas.p: On flat ground, what is the ZMP in classical controllers?
opcoes: The same point as the center of mass of the whole robot.
The highest point of the robot, which on the G1 is the head.
The center of pressure: the average of the contacts weighted by force.
The joint that produces the most torque during the push on the torso.
perguntas.explica: On flat ground, ZMP and center of pressure coincide. The CoM is something else: it can leave the polygon; the CoP cannot.

perguntas.p: 40 N for 0.1 s does not knock it over; 40 N for 0.2 s does. What does this teach?
opcoes: That the duration of the push changes nothing in the result.
That MuJoCo becomes unstable when the push is too short and too strong.
That 40 N is the exact limit the real G1 can take while standing.
That the impulse (force × time) is what counts for the fall.
perguntas.explica: 4 N·s does not knock it over, 8 N·s does, with 40 N or with 80 N. And none of this is the limit of the real G1: there is no balance controller here.

itens.texto: CoM, support polygon and CoP come out of the model at every step.
Leaving the support is rotating; falling is rotating too fast to come back.
Without a controller, the G1 takes 15 N for 0.2 s and falls with 35 N.
